title: LingBot-Vision: Boundary-Aware Self-Supervised Pretraining
hook: Masked-patch pretraining hopes boundary structure emerges on its own. This method forces the issue, masking exactly the regions a student can't infer by copying context — and beats a 7B model at 1.1B.
key_points: Standard masked-image pretraining masks random patches and hopes boundary/edge structure emerges as a side effect.

LingBot-Vision instead has the teacher predict a dense boundary field online, then forces the boundary-bearing tokens into the student's mask — so the student must reconstruct exactly the regions that can't be inferred by copying nearby context.
Boundary targets come from the teacher itself, not external labels or an edge detector.
At 1.1B parameters, reaches 0.296 NYUv2 linear-probe RMSE, beating DINOv3-7B's 0.309 — with roughly 6x fewer parameters — though it trails on ImageNet.
Weights released in four model sizes.
content_html: Self-supervised pretraining usually masks random patches and trusts that useful structure — like object boundaries — will emerge as a side effect of reconstruction. LingBot-Vision instead targets boundaries directly, on purpose.
extra_html: The teacher model predicts a dense boundary field online, and those specific boundary-bearing tokens get forced into the student's mask — meaning the student can't cheat by copying nearby unmasked context, since the masked regions are exactly the ones that can't be inferred that way. The boundary targets come from the teacher itself, rather than external labels or a hand-built edge detector, and get recast as per-pixel categorical distributions so the same centering and sharpening machinery used elsewhere in the self-distillation setup applies to the geometric branch too. The payoff shows up in linear-probe transfer: at 1.1 billion parameters, LingBot-Vision reaches 0.296 RMSE on NYUv2 depth, edging out DINOv3-7B's 0.309 with roughly six times fewer parameters — though it trails DINOv3 on ImageNet classification. Weights are released in four sizes. Posted to r/MachineLearning, 2026-07-06.
